articles.summary: El GOAT del Trial desglosa las claves de un año verdaderamente histórico por la redondo de la cifra. El de Piera ha llegado a un punto en el que atesora más coronas que años...
articles.body: A estas alturas de la película, con Toni Bou (Piera, Barcelona, 17 de octubre de 1986) se han agotado los adjetivos calificativos. El pasado fin de semana, el competidor del Repsol Honda HRC selló, de forma matemática, su 40ª corona mundial de trial en la ronda de los Países Bajos. En la cita de Zelhem, el piloto de la Montesa Cota 4RT abrochó una temporada (a la que le resta un gran premio) marcada por una lesión que al final no le ha impedido lucirse tanto en la modalidad Indoor (20 entorchados) como en la disciplina Outdoor (otros 20). Y en el compartimento estanco de victorias parciales también anda sobrado: 275 (99 bajo techo y 176 al aire libre). A sus 39 abriles, el GOAT del Trial atesora más títulos mundiales que años. Un hecho insólito que evidencia la magnitud de un talento especial que se ha ganado el derecho a codearse con las más grandes leyendas de cualquier especialidad deportiva. PREGUNTA: ¿Con qué palabra definiría su corona número 40º? Hemos escuchado mucho estos días: increíble, histórico, brutal... Esos son los vocablos más usados. ¿Cuál sería el que elegiría para autodefinirse? RESPUESTA: Buena pregunta. Diría orgullo. Emoción. Ha sido muy emocionante. P: ¿Cómo ha sido competir con el hándicap físico del hombro derecho lastimado? R: La verdad es que fue muy complicado el inicio, sobre todo los primeros tres meses, fueron súper difíciles para mí porque me sentía muy mal encima de la moto, iba consiguiendo resultados, me alimentaba un poco de los resultados, pero sabía que no podía seguir de esta manera. Pero es verdad que después del tercer mes, al cuarto mes hubo un cambio. Empezamos a trabajar un poco diferente, intentando buscar evitar el dolor en cada entrenamiento, en cada sesión de gimnasio con el fisio, donde entrenamos un poco diferente. Eso también me ayudó mucho. Empecé a descansar mucho mejor por las noches y evidentemente el tendón está roto, pero ha funcionado de otra manera. Me empecé a divertir también en los entrenamientos y eso provocó un cambio bestial en la temporada. P: ¿Cómo lleva lo de atesorar más títulos que años? R: Estoy sorprendido. La verdad es que ni yo mismo me esperaba llegar hasta aquí. Siempre lo he dicho, me dedico a lo que más me gusta. Y he conseguido mucho más de lo que yo me podía llegar a imaginar. 20 y 30 eran cifras increíbles, pero esto es más por lo de llevar 20 años consecutivos ganando los dos títulos. Encima, ahora cumplir 40 años justo después de ganar el 40º título es algo espectacular. P: ¿Según ganó el 40, ya estaba pensando en el 41? R: Ya sabes que yo siempre pienso un poco en ir más allá. Pero sí que es verdad que este tengo muchas ganas de disfrutar este 40º título, de tomármelo con calma. Aparte tenemos como tres meses ahora hasta empezar el próximo campeonato. Hay tiempo para meditar y disfrutarlo. Es lo que toca y seguro que lo haremos así. No obstante, es cierto que no dejas de pensarlo nunca. Siempre pasa por la cabeza. Y eso es lo que me ha llevado hasta aquí. P: Una pregunta recurrente: ¿Hasta cuándo, Toni? El siguiente Everest es las 50 coronas... R: Vamos a ver qué sucede con la lesión. La verdad es que me cuesta ahora verme cinco años más compitiendo. Vamos a ver el hombro cómo va reaccionando, qué decidimos también con los médicos. Puede ser que que pierda algún campeonato. No lo descarto si me opero, pero también tengo muchas cosas en mente. Tengo ganas de lograr más récords, como lo que hicimos junto a Repsol en Piera, en mi pueblo. Hacer más vídeos e intentar que mi pilotaje llegue a todo el mundo. Son cosas que también me motivan, que vamos a intentar combinar también con los próximos campeonatos. P: Obviamente, es consciente de que si pierde es más noticia que si gana... R: Sí, claro está. Desde hace ya muchos años si pierdo es mucho más noticia que si gano. Pero ahora sí que después de este título, aún más. P: ¿Cómo es posible lograr este milagro de ganar tantos años seguidos que es lo que más sorprende? No que gane, sino la consistencia de ganar tantos años seguidos. R: Yo creo que lo que más ha marcado mi carrera siempre es esas ganas de querer más y más y de no cambiar mi mentalidad. No, no es que lo haya trabajado, sino es que soy así. He encontrado siempre la motivación en los momentos complicados, en los momentos donde no hay motivación. En el deporte muchas veces cuando ya lo has conseguido todo seguir es muy difícil. Y creo que esa mentalidad de ganar y competir contra mí mismo cada día, en cada entrenamiento es lo que me ha llevado hasta aquí. P: ¿Cómo era Toni Bou hace 20 años y como es ahora? ¿En qué ha cambiado? R: Pues te diría que hace 20 años era muy diferente, pero me parezco en muchas cosas. Evidentemente que lo más importante no lo he cambiado. He seguido siendo ese piloto y esa persona que es muy tranquila en casa y muy agresiva en las carreras, donde intenta no tirar la toalla hasta el último minuto, hasta el último segundo. Y eso creo que es lo más importante. He mantenido esa garra de querer lucharlo todo, hasta el último momento y eso es lo que me ha llevado hasta aquí. P: En 2019 logró un pleno de victorias, algo que puede lograr este curso si vence en el TrialGP de Pobladura de las Regueras. ¿Si sale victorioso sería esta su mejor temporada? R: Si pudiera conseguir el pleno de esta temporada, quizá te diría que sí. En 2026 se me ha dado todo muy bien. En verdad, no sé si sería la mejor, pero seguro que sí una de las dos mejores temporadas de mi vida y eso es algo que me llena mucho. Y más con la lesión que he tenido. P: ¿Le fastidia mucho no poder acabar el Outdoor habiendo ganado todos los puntos? R: Pues la verdad es que no, estoy muy tranquilo. No pasa nada por no tener esos tres puntitos y quedarme sin el pleno de puntos en el campeonato. Pero también te digo que he ganado muchas carreras por muy poquito, donde a otros rivales los he ganado por la mínima. Y tampoco creo que mereciera la victoria (que se embolsó Jaime Busto) porque cometí un error muy grande en la segunda vuelta. Así que muy contento con acabar ganando el día, que también era algo que quería más que ganar todos los puntos, sino poder celebrar la victoria, el campeonato con una victoria del día. P: Cambiando de tercio, ¿ve ganando a Marc Márquez el décimo título? R: Marc tiene una lesión muy grave y creo que está sufriendo muchísimo, pero también estoy convencido de que acabará ganando este título. He hablado mucho con él, lo veo con confianza, con una situación que tiene que manejarla muy bien, aprovechar muy bien sus oportunidades, Pero creo que de aquí a final de temporada aún va a crecer más y se merece ese título más que nadie. P: En clave de Fórmula 1, Fernando Alonso tiene 45 años y este año está compitiendo con un coche poco competitivo. ¿Cómo se sentiría en su situación? R: Cómo lo está gestionando dice mucho de Fernando. También es uno de mis ídolos y me gusta mucho su forma de afrontar las cosas. Creo que ha seguido porque siente que puede demostrar su valía y si un día, en este deporte que depende tanto del coche, le llega un F1 diferencial donde él pueda demostrar el gran piloto que es, porque es uno de los mejores, podrá volver a luchar por un campeonato. Así que entiendo que siga al pie del cañón y comparto su postura. P: ¿Cuál es la felicitación que más ilusión le ha hecho? R: Este año han sido muchísimas. Desde amigos que siempre me felicitan a otros no tan habituales. Me ha hecho mucha ilusión ver una felicitación diferente porque es un título diferente. Me ha emocionado más que otros años. Evidentemente, me ha encantado la celebración del equipo. Y ese vídeo con mis ídolos y mis amigos me ha emocionado. Significa mucho ser reconocido por tan grandes deportistas. Ha sido algo espectacular. P: Lleva 99 victorias en el Indoor. Tiene una motivación extra porque la temporada que viene ya puede ser centenario... R: Sí, los números siempre están ahí alentándome, siempre hay motivaciones. Ahora, el número 100. Sinceramente, no pensaba que llegaría a esto. Antaño hacíamos campeonatos de cuatro o cinco carreras y es muy difícil llegar a 100 victorias. Así que estamos sólo a una. No lo dejaremos aquí. Intentaremos luchar por conseguir también en el 50º aniversario del Indoor de Barcelona, mi victoria número 20. Estamos con 19 victorias. Siempre hay retos, siempre hay cosas. Ya me conoces, nunca paro mentalmente. P: La última. ¿Va a hacer alguna celebración especial por ser el título 40? R: Vamos a hacer una celebración súper especial y voy a intentar esperar que estén todos mis amigos, juntar a toda mi gente y hacer una celebración que también sea histórica.

articles.title: Cristina Gutiérrez ya tiene coche para el Dakar 2027: ficha por Santana y estrena copiloto
articles.standfirst: La burgalesa inicia una nueva etapa en la Baja Aragón, con el Santana y con Marc Solá a su derecha
articles.summary: La burgalesa inicia una nueva etapa en la Baja Aragón, con el Santana y con Marc Solá a su derecha
articles.body: La puerta de Dacia se le cerró a Cristina Gutiérrez... pero ahora se le ha abierto la de Santana. La burgalesa será piloto oficial de la marca andaluza en el próximo Dakar 2027, pero debutará al volante de su nuevo prototipo antes. De hecho, en apenas unos días, en la Baja España Aragón (11 al 13 de septiembre). Gutiérrez, además, tendrá un nuevo compañero de viaje para esta aventura: Marc Solá. El catalán, ex piloto de motos con Himoinsa, ha disputado los últimos Dakar al lado de Carlos Checa en el Astara Team y del chef Nandu Jubany en su proyecto en coches. Ahora será el nuevo navegante de la ganadora del Dakar 2024 en SxS tomando el relevo de Pablo Moreno Huete. “Estoy muy ilusionada de unirme al Santana Racing Team para afrontar dos carreras tan exigentes como la Baja España-Aragón y el Rally de Marruecos. Conozco muy bien ambas pruebas, pero el Santana Pick-Up T1+ es nuevo para mí y Marc y yo necesitaremos adaptarnos rápidamente al vehículo para poder luchar por buenas posiciones. Unirme a la familia Santana es especial, ya que, además de un origen, compartimos una pasión por el off-road que da sentido a lo que somos”, explica la burgalesa... que se medirá a sus ex compañeros de Dacia en el Rally de Marruecos. Eso sí, con una máquina diferente: el Santana Pick-Up que el año pasado tripularon el aventurero Jesús Calleja y el CEO de la marca española, Edu Blanco. Recordemos que se trata de un Century CR7 de la categoría reina recarrozado y puesto a punto por Santana, un vehículo competitivo capaz de pelear por el top 10 en las etapas del Dakar. Cristina Gutiérrez hereda el puesto del aventurero leonés, que a día de hoy no disputará el próximo Dakar aunque sigue unido a Santana como director deportivo. Un fichaje de campanillas que, como no podía ser de otro modo, saluda también el CEO de Santana Motors, Edu Blanco. "Es difícil describir a Cristina, toda una campeona del Dakar: su forma de ser, su espíritu de superación y capacidad de adaptación, su increíble talento y su palmarés hablan por sí mismos. A su lado tendremos a un valor seguro, Marc Solà, piloto y copiloto de rally, campeón de enduro y un excelente navegante formado en la que probablemente sea la mejor escuela para esta tarea: las motos. En su estreno como piloto de Santana Gutiérrez coincidirá, además, con sus compatriotas Marta y Mónica Plaza, que también correrán la Baja Aragón con el Santana SUV T1 con el que han completado el CERTT - GT2i. Después, tendrá un test más exigente en el Rally de Marruecos ((26 de septiembre-3 de octubre), la penúltima cita del Mundial de Rally Raid W2RC.

articles.title: IndyCar champ Alex Palou on the importance of appreciating success after his fourth straight series title
articles.summary: Alex Palou tells OutKick he pinches himself daily over his four consecutive IndyCar titles with Chip Ganassi Racing and what drives the team's fire.
articles.body: For the fifth time in six years — and the fourth year straight — Chip Ganassi Racing's Alex Palou is the NTT IndyCar Series champion. It's an incredible run, with only Sébastien Bourdais matching his four-straight title run, having done so in the mid-2000s before the Indy Racing League and the Champ Car World Series merger. But while he's far from a stranger when it comes to winning championships, Palou told OutKick over Zoom on Monday that he's always taking time to appreciate his successes. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSIBLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "Every single day, man, like, almost every single day," Palou said. "I kind of need to pinch myself and be like, 'It's incredible to be in this position.' I never thought in my entire life that I would have an opportunity like this. I'm just trying to enjoy as much as I can because I know at some point it's going to end, right? And there's going to be someone else sitting in this seat, in this chair, and I just want to make sure I take it all in." Palou's run has been incredible, especially in a series renowned for its competitive balance and the need to master three totally different styles of racetrack. As much as that comes down to Palou, it also comes down to the environment at CGR and the people who have worked to get the No. 10 Honda to victory lane for so many years. "It's very tough to stay up top... and the thing I like the most is the fire that everybody has at Chip Ganassi Racing," the 29-year-old from Spain said. "Although they have already won 18 championships, there's people that are in my car who have been for each one of those 18 championships, and they still work as much as they can to make sure that we can continue to battle and fight for the championship." That team is about to see a big change as Palou's longtime teammate Scott Dixon will move to Arrow McLaren in 2027 after 25 years with CGR. While the new driver of the No. 9 has yet to be announced at the time of writing, Palou will likely be the most experienced driver on the team, which also includes Kyffin Simpson in the No. 8. Still, he doesn't expect to see his role on the team change in any way. "I don't think it's going to change much, honestly. Like, I think the way we have of working at Chip Ganassi Racing," Palou said. "There's not a lead driver that kind of manages a bit more than everybody else or has more say." He said that he expected it to work that way, especially in his first season on the team when he was driving alongside not just Dixon, but another bona fide motorsports legend: NASCAR great Jimmie Johnson. "So I thought that I had like zero say on how we were going to operate and how we were going to prepare the cars and stuff, and that was not the case," he explained. "They treated me like another one like them. I had the same (input) as they did, and I think nowadays it works the same way with Kyffin... whoever is fastest at practice, that's the leader of the team that day." INDYCAR'S FREEDOM 250 GRAND PRIX SPECTACLE IN WASHINGTON, DC DRAWS MASSIVE TV RATINGS Looking to the future, Palou isn't just chasing more championships; he's also going to have a big part in the future of the series. He was front and center at the series' marquee events, including the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, a massive success for the series. "It was a big win for IndyCar, and also that showed what we're able to achieve," he said, before joking that maybe hitting the highs of last month's race around the Nation's capital were lofty. "I think that was a 12 out of 10 as an event in general." But the series is in a good place and will only get better with the introduction of its first new chassis in well over a decade, the Dallara IR-28. Palou tested the new car on the Indianapolis Motor Speedway in August, and is set to give it a shakedown on the track's iconic oval on Thursday. The early returns are very good. "I mean, it was incredible," he said. "I would love to race it next year instead of in '28, but honestly, I think everyone at IndyCar and both engine manufacturers, Honda (and Chevrolet), have done incredible work on developing this new car. We had like almost zero issues." He then pointed out that this car has more than a year of development before it makes its in-race debut in 2028. "I think, already now, if the car was on track with the other IndyCars, that car would win the race by far," he explained. "So, yeah, I'm excited to see what we're able to do and achieve with the car if we work for a full year." articles.title: NASCAR WTT Raceway Schedule: TV Channels, Start Times and How to Watch
articles.summary: The NASCAR Cup Series heads to the World Wide Technology Raceway this Sunday for the Enjoy Illinois 300.
articles.body:
NASCAR heads to the World Wide Technology Raceway, formerly known as Gateway Motorsports Park, this weekend for doubleheader action. The Cup Series and the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series will take to the 1.25-mile track, the second race of the Chase for both series.

For the Cup Series, it is the fifth time the circuit has raced on the Madison, Illinois track, which is within 10 minutes of St. Louis. Meanwhile, the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series has raced at WTT Raceway since 1997.

Here is a full breakdown of the weekend schedule and how to watch all the on-track action from WTT Raceway.

1:00 pm. ET O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Practice TV: ESPN Unlimited

1:00 pm. ET O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Practice

2:05 p.m. ET: O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Qualifying TV: ESPN Unlimited

2:05 p.m. ET: O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Qualifying

3:30 p.m. ET: Cup Series Practice TV: TruTV Radio: Motor Racing Network (MRN), SiriusXM Satellite

Radio: Motor Racing Network (MRN), SiriusXM Satellite

4:35 p.m. ET: Cup Series Qualifying TV: TruTV Radio: MRN, SiriusXM Satellite

7:30 p.m. ET: O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Nu Way 225 Powered by Bobcat and Sauced by Blues Hog TV: The CW, ESPN Unlimited Radio: MRN, SiriusXM Satellite

7:30 p.m. ET: O'Reilly Auto Parts Series Nu Way 225 Powered by Bobcat and Sauced by Blues Hog

5:00 p.m. ET: NASCAR Cup Series Enjoy Illinois 300 TV: USA Network Radio: MRN, SiriusXM Satellite Stream: HBO Max Driver Cam

5:00 p.m. ET: NASCAR Cup Series Enjoy Illinois 300

For fans who prefer a TV broadcast, USA Network for the Cup Series and The CW for the O'Reilly Auto Parts Series are the go-to channels. However, for fans who like a closer look at the action, HBO Max Driver Cam gives them that opportunity.

HBO provides an up-close look at NASCAR Cup Series action with on-board cameras for every Cup driver in the field, with an HBO Max subscription of standard or higher. The service also provides driver/team radio audio to further enhance the experience.

Denny Hamlin enters Sunday's Enjoy Illinois 300 as the defending winner. The driver of the No. 11 started on the pole and paced the field for a race-high 75 of 240 laps en route to his 59th career Cup victory. It marked Hamlin's fourth of five wins in 2025.

The win, under the previous playoff format, earned the Joe Gibbs Racing driver a spot in the Round of 12. The 45-year-old proceeded to advance to the Championship 4 race and was within three laps of claiming his first Cup Series title.

Yet, a caution followed by a deferring pit strategy shuffled Hamlin back, allowing Kyle Larson to win the title.

This Sunday, Hamlin is seeking his 65th career Cup victory and his fifth of the 2026 season. The Virginia native leads the Chase standings with a 12-point advantage over Christopher Bell, who moved into second after his win in the Cook Out Southern 500.

articles.title: "Hamilton y Leclerc tienen que hablar no sólo con Vasseur, sino con alguien superior"
articles.standfirst: Montoya cree que la alta dirección de Ferrari debe mediar entre ambos. Muchas crítricas a la gestión del galo en los medios italianos
articles.summary: Montoya cree que la alta dirección de Ferrari debe mediar entre ambos. Muchas crítricas a la gestión del galo en los medios italianos
articles.body: Juan Pablo Montoya cree que en Ferrari se le está yendo de las manos la rivalidad entre Hamilton y Leclerc, después del la acción en la primera chicane de Monza, en la que el monegasco arrinconó a su compañero y lo mandó a la gravilla sexto puesto. El '16' sufrió un accidente poco después y Lewis ya no se recuperó en toda la carrera del lance, pero porque el coche no se lo permitió tampoco. En declaraciones a F1 TV tras la carrera, Hamilton, que actualmente ocupa el tercer puesto en el campeonato de pilotos, admitió que el resultado fue "difícil de digerir". Durante la retransmisión, al analizar la carrera de Ferrari, Montoya argumentó que el director del equipo, Fred Vasseur, y la alta dirección deben reunirse con ambos pilotos antes del Gran Premio de España de este fin de semana en Madrid. "Tienen que hablar no solo con Fred, sino con alguien superior a él. Ambos tienen que ir a Maranello esta semana y sentarse a conversar seriamente porque, en mi opinión, Charles dijo: 'Competí contra Lewis como lo habría hecho contra cualquier otro'", explicó Montoya. Para él no es una actitud constructiva. Leclerc, sin embargo, estuvo de pruebas médicas en Mónaco, tras su choque de 23 G en la Parabólica de la vuelta 2. "Es tu compañero y tienes que respetar a tu compañero de equipo, y tienes que respetar al equipo", remataba el expiloto colombiano. Las criticas por el rendimiento y la gestión de los pilotos de la Scuderia, han arreciado en los medios italianos. Vasseur tiene un ratio de 8 victorias en 83 GP al frente de Ferrari y para muchos no es suficiente. Y más después de ver lo que pasó en Mercedes, donde Antonelli fue separado de Russell tras la primera remontada y se le pusieron gomas frescas para que ambos no estuvieran en igualdad de condiciones. En todo caso, el italiano parecía imbatible desde el inicio de la carrera, después de enjugar 18 puestos en las 18 vueltas iniciales. Se vuelve a poner en cuestión al ingeniero francés, una vez que Lewis queda descolgado de la lucha por el Mundial, a nada menos que 78 puntos de Antonelli.

articles.title: Max Verstappen interview: Red Bull driver on McLaren talks, 'numb' cars and why he speaks his mind
articles.summary: In an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, Max Verstappen talks about his new contract at Red Bull and much more.
articles.body:
Max Verstappen is in a no-nonsense mood - even more than usual.

The Red Bull driver is renowned for his straight talking but now, as he discusses his 2026 season so far in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, he is at his most uncompromising.

We're talking on the eve of last weekend's Italian Grand Prix. The temperature is into the mid-30Cs, Red Bull's hospitality unit is not coping well, and Verstappen's PR handler messages before the Dutchman turns up to suggest I find a table near a fan; the interview might be more positive that way.

Monza is the second race since the four-time world champion signed a two-year contract extension with Red Bull.

In theory, this runs to the end of 2030. In reality, it changes little. It still has performance clauses. So Verstappen is earning a bit more money but, if Red Bull are still struggling for competitiveness next year, there will remain the prospect he could look for pastures new.

Verstappen arrives and briefly adjusts the fan blowing in our direction. "It's too hot in here," he says.

Does he need a breather before we start? "No, no," he says. "I'm good. It was just that it was super-hot in the corner when I was doing the print [media]."

Verstappen is always a great interviewee. Direct, honest, uncompromising.

Now, for whatever reason, he is especially frank and open, as we discuss why he extended his contract, his discussions with McLaren, his stunning appearance at the Nurburgring 24 Hours in May, and the new Formula 1 engine rules, with which it is no secret he has a problem.

Where's your head at, Max, in terms of how the season has gone so far?

"Of course it's not where I want to be, but as a team we're trying to just learn and understand a lot of things for next year. We are not in a title fight. We are just trying to find more performance.

"Changes need to happen to the car for next year. We will not be able to change that for this year, but we just need to try and get a lot of learnings to do better next year."

"Overall we're just lacking a bit of performance. The car is not where I want it to be feeling-wise, and the through-corner balance is too hit and miss between entry, mid and exit.

"It's just fundamentally something in the car that we need to try and work on for the next year."

This has been a bit of a theme for longer than this year. How concerning is it that that's happening across a different set of regulations?

"That's exactly that. There's also things that we talk about within the team, like how can that happen, how can we fix it? That's basically what we are doing now and trying to do now.

"Some people have left, new people have come in. With the new people, we are discussing what we can do about it. Is that just some changes, a different philosophy? All these kind of things."

"It comes down to also feeling well within a team. This is like a second family to me.

"The belief that you can turn things around, you can build towards hopefully a better future with other people, new people. And at the end of the day, it's not only Formula 1 for me. There are a lot of things that I'm doing next year that Red Bull is involved in as well.

"I feel good here. So this, for me, is the right place to be."

Did it take much for them to convince you to do it?

"I always said to them: 'Don't stress about it, just work on the car.' Because the faster the car goes, the easier the decision is anyway.

"I can understand, of course, maybe sometimes they were a little bit worried. But at the same time, for me, I was just worried about here, what was going on.

"At the same time, I was very busy with my stuff also outside of Formula 1. So I never really spent a lot of time talking or doing different things or trying to go somewhere else."

From the outside, it's hard to see what they could have done to convince you things will improve.

"I don't mind the challenge also. I don't have that desire or need to show in another car that I can win it, or whatever.

"It's easy to run to the fastest car and then do it all again. But it's not how I am. You cannot be the captain of the ship and as soon as there is something not working, you jump off the ship.

"It's been a bit downwards from the dominant years, but I don't mind also rebuilding it. It's another challenge as well."

You talked to Mercedes last year, McLaren this year. How serious was that?

"Of course, any kind of chat you take seriously. They're all very respectful chats. There's nothing wrong with that.

"I felt that staying was, for me, the right choice. You have to follow your heart. I could have run away very early on in my Red Bull career and gone somewhere else to try and win. If you have a little bit of patience, you do end up winning. I feel like that's my approach now as well."

What race have you enjoyed most this year?

"Probably the Nordschleife [Nurburgring 24 Hours]. It was super-cool to be able to do an endurance event with my team-mates, the guys that won with the car throughout the main season.

"We knew that we were going to be really strong. We peaked at the right time, but unfortunately the car retired. It was an incredible experience. And pure. Pure motorsport."

Your first stint, where you went from 10th to first, was so impressive.

"I was enjoying it. Not easy conditions. It started to drizzle. The track was slippery. Crashes. Code 60s [when a stretch of track is limited to 60km/h after an incident].

"Some people were like: 'Let's see how he will do in the race under pressure with all these kinds of scenarios that he has never done before.'

"But I have done them a million times on the simulator. I have done so many laps and 24-hour races on the simulator. I never felt out of depth or whatever. I was fully zoned in. I just had a great time.

"Once I was in the race, you switch to another level. I was just in a zone. It's really enjoyable."

You want to go back to Nurburgring to win that race. Is there anything else on your bucket list?

"All the endurance races. Eventually, of course also Hypercar [the world endurance championship]. I don't want to rush it. I want to do it in the right environment. On my terms. And competitive."

Is it true you want to do Le Mans with Fernando Alonso?

"We've talked about it. I mean, look at Fernando. He's 45 and he's still flying. Especially for Le Mans, with his experience, it could be a good option. It needs to fit our schedules. It needs to make sense. It needs to be on my terms. And there needs to be a real chance to go there and win it."

You have been clear about your distaste for the new F1 engine rules this year and at the Japanese Grand Prix you said: 'Is it worth it?' What convinced you it was?

"Hoping that it will be better in the future. Accepting where we are at the moment. Still the love for the sport. Not at the moment the driving. But the love for the sport.

"I love competition, naturally. I just hope that in the coming years, towards 2030, it can only get better. And to start to make the best of it, because these are the rules for the next four or five years."

So that people can understand why the drivers have been upset this year, what is it about these hybrid engines, and the need to recharge the batteries, that detracts from the best drivers' abilities?

"In the history of the sport, normally the driver that is the most committed, the latest on the brakes, earlier on throttle, committing in the high speed, they get rewarded, because you just gain that time in the corner.

"But now you're constantly thinking about, 'In this corner I might have to hold in a bit. Go later on throttle. Or brake earlier. Or lift off. And then I have more top speed.' Stuff like that. It's so unnatural. It's so not how it should be.

"No disrespect. And I hope no-one picks up on this. But look at Yuki [Tsunoda]. He jumps in the [Racing Bulls] car [at the Dutch Grand Prix]. Never driven the car before. Immediately competitive.

"Liam [Lawson] jumps from the Racing Bulls to the Red Bull - immediately competitive. It's because these cars are numb to your driver inputs.

"Of course, yes, you still have to do a good lap. And you still have to commit. The fastest drivers will always come out on top. But it's really, really limited, like a choke hold or something. You're held back."

Formula 1 as a sport has accepted that it needs to change, and the internal combustion-electrical split is changing to 60-40 in two steps by 2028. But what would you like to see for the new engine formula 1 in 2030 or 2031?

"It has to go back to a V8, just for drivability already. When you drive the old cars, you cannot imagine the difference in how the engine responds, or the drivability you get. And how terrible or horrible it actually is now compared to just having a V8."

What about compared to last year's turbo-hybrid engines?

"Also horrible, the feeling compared to a V8. The V8 is so much better. It is so much more free, lighter. Cars are so heavy nowadays.

"It is better to just have a smaller V8 engine, much lighter. Try to really limit the battery size to maybe like a kind of push-to-pass battery. But you should not have it involved or any kind of proper normal performance running."

"Ideally not, because that introduces turbo lag."

So what do you enjoy about F1 these days? The competition and prestige more than the actual purity of the racing?

"I have been lucky that the years before have been quite decent [in terms of results]. Not how I wanted it to be with the battery side of things.

"But just the emotion of the V8, of the V10, back in the day, when I was a kid. You walk around, you hear these cars go out, you have goosebumps.

"Even if you go 300km/h compared to now sometimes 350, 360, it doesn't matter.

"It is the emotion of the noise that you get from these cars, of the vibration. It is just another level. And I really hope that that thing will come back."

People see you as a kind of winning machine. But obviously your character is much more complex than that. Can you explain that contradiction?

"I am a winning machine when I need to be. But I can also switch off, and enjoy my life outside of racing.

"But anything racing-related, of course I am a winning machine. I demand a lot from the people in the team. They also expect me to perform and do the best job I can.

"That is what you get paid for at the end of the day. We have the same target. The same goal.

"Of course I can be very outspoken. But that is what I like. That is also with our culture.

"And that is how I approach my life also outside of F1, with my GT3 team. We do not hold back. At least for me, you need to be like that to really get the best out of everyone."

Why is speaking your mind and being honest so important to you?

"I just want to be myself. I know there are a lot of politics in Formula 1, and I understand also between the teams there are a lot of politics.

"You will always speak for yourself in terms of where you think you might have an advantage or not as a team. That is normal. Also with the engines and the chassis, it is the same thing.

"When it is good, it is good. When it is bad, it is bad. You will hear it from me because that is how I like to operate. And I am not holding back from that."

articles.summary: In Wednesday's feature race, the prolific hurdler Loriko looks to continue a successful spell for the Skelton team in a fascinating contest at Sedgefield; we have seven races in all, live on Sky Sports Racing from 2pm
articles.body:
4.00 Sedgefield - Skelton's in-form Loriko headlines

Dan Skelton's in-form Loriko tops five runners for the feature Sedgefield Racecourse For Outdoor Events Handicap Hurdle .

Loriko has shown improved form this season, winning three of his five starts, including when narrowly landing a novice hurdle at Market Rasen last month. He looks to have strong claims as he steps up in trip on this switch to handicap company.

Ladies Day has taken well to hurdling and Tom Ellis' five-year-old looks an obvious threat. She travelled well when fading into fourth at Cartmel and might appreciate the extra yardage here.

Glory And Honour showed he still retains all his ability when just denied here last time and rates the pick of the remainder.

5.05 Sedgefield - Saint Polo and Pergamon clash

Progressive pair Saint Polo and Pergamon do battle in a cracking renewal of this Whitegates Nursery Northallerton Handicap Hurdle at Sedgefield.

The Jennie Candlish-trained Saint Polo returned from a break to complete the hat-trick at this venue last month taking his record to three wins from four stars with cheekpieces fitted. Up another three pounds, he can go close under Luke Scott.

Pergamon is another who arrives in super form having scored on his last three starts over hurdles. He has now won five of his eight outings over jumps and must be feared providing the ground remains on the good side.

King Ulanda capitalised on a lower hurdles mark when taking a Uttoxeter handicap back in July and is another to consider.

3.00 Sedgefield - Last-time winners Glenmalure Flyer and Limerick Leader headline

Last-time winners Glenmalure Flyer and Limerick Leader headline a field of Christmas Parties At Sedgefield Racecourse Handicap Chase at Sedgefield.

Glenmalure Flyer has landed two of his three runs since joining Dan Skelton from David Nagle and looks to have an excellent chance of following up his recent Stratford success. He relishes a strong stamina test and might be able to dominate this small field.

Nick Scholfield's Limerick Leader doubled his tally over fences when landing a three-mile handicap chase at Bangor but will need to show he can back that up with the longer distance a concern.

Sir Carnegie and Thank You Blue complete the quartet.

11.17 Kentucky Downs - Listed Juvenile Mile - Joseph O'Brien fields Otherworldly and One Number .

11.49 Kentucky Downs - La Fogata represents Donnacha. Kentucky Belle has looked progressive.

2.00 Sedgefield - Interesting maiden hurdle to open proceedings.

articles.title: Spanish GP: What to expect from new Madring track in Madrid with Carlos Sainz predicting safety cars and red flags
articles.summary: The Madring street circuit in Madrid is set to be a huge challenge for the drivers as Formula 1 enters the unknown this weekend; watch every session of the Spanish Grand Prix at a new track in Madrid from this Friday, live on Sky Sports F1
articles.body:
The Spanish Grand Prix has moved from its traditional circuit in Barcelona to a high-speed street track in Madrid and has been described as "Jeddah on steroids" by Formula 3 drivers who tested there last month - the Jeddah track itself is one of the most challenging circuits in F1.

So why is the Madring so difficult and how will it impact the racing we see this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1 ?

There are 22 official corners on the 3.365-mile Madring circuit, although unusually the track layout has Turns 5A and 20A - so maybe there are 24.

Whatever the number, after the start/finish straight the driver will almost always be turning the steering wheel at some point as there are few straights.

The left-right chicane of Turns 1 and 2 is one of just a few overtaking spots thanks to its heavy braking zone before a long blast through Turns 3 and 4 towards arguably the most awkward chicane in F1 since the old 'Singapore Sling' chicane which was used at the Singapore Grand Prix between 2008 and 2012.

Just how much speed and how much kerb the drivers can use at Turn 5 will be a critical point of the circuit. If cars go side by side approaching Turn 5, hold your breath, because you cannot fit two cars through there alongside each other. However, the long flat-out zone before the chicane means drivers will be keen to make an overtake here...

After that, the track goes up and down into a really tricky uphill braking zone of Turn 7 where we may see drivers glancing the barriers on the outside.

The track then veers left, right and left, which may be flat out come qualifying when the track is clean after plenty of rubber has gone down from the practice sessions.

Then comes, what could become iconic, Turn 12, known as La Monumental. A huge banked corner that turns 180 degrees at 24 per cent gradient (13.5 degrees) where the drivers will try to stay hard on the throttle as much as possible while experiencing massive G-forces.

After a left-hand flick at Turn 13, the next few corners should be flat out until you arrive at a 90-degree right hander of Turn 17 before the drivers dance through Turns 18 and 19 at high speed, then hit the brakes into a sharp left hander at Turn 20.

The last corner of Turn 22 is a 90-degree right hander where the inside barriers jut out, so the drivers will need to be careful not to cut the apex too much as they arrive on the main straight to complete a rollercoaster lap which should be around 90 seconds in qualifying.

Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, plus Williams' Carlos Sainz are the only drivers to have any experience of driving the circuit.

Sainz is a Madring ambassador and gave input on the Turn 12 La Monumental banking so track designers could ensure it is safe, while still being unique.

Leclerc said: "It's a very, very special corner. It's a corner where I feel in qualifying, we'll have to, I will say it in a polite way, but we'll have to be very brave because it's going to be on the limit.

"And so that's going to be really cool, I think. It's going to be a really cool corner. I do believe it can become one of the most iconic corners of the season, especially once the grandstand will be built. I think that will add also to the experience of that corner."

Leclerc and Hamilton conducted a filming day in July when the track had only just finished its completion, so it was extremely hot and dusty.

"As you would expect, there was no grip. So your tyres were basically just covered in dust, and that's the whole time," said Hamilton.

"It looks like it will be a qualifying lap sort of circuit, and there's not really any straights. So it looks like a difficult place to overtake."

For much of the track, if the drivers are slightly off the racing line by turning at the wrong time or carrying a little too much speed, they could easily find themselves in the barriers at high speed.

The risk-versus-reward stakes will be very high and the bravest drivers, who get it right, will come out on top.

"I think definitely with the way they've put the barriers and the design of the track it's going to be one of the biggest challenges in Formula 1 recently," said Sainz.

"The track reminds me a lot of Jeddah, it reminds me a lot of Baku, even reminds me a bit of Macau in some ways. So having that in an F1 [car] with 1,000 horsepower is going to be quite an interesting challenge, so let's see how it goes."

So we are going to get safety cars and red flags?

In short, almost certainly. Such is the difficulty of the track, it is a question of how many red flags will we see across practice, qualifying and the race. As we saw at the Italian Grand Prix, if any barriers need to be repaired for crashes, that will definitely require a red flag.

In the two-day F3 test, there were 19 red flags - albeit not all of them were for crashes.

"Looking at the track and hearing of what happened in the F3 test, I think we are all expecting safety cars, red flags and yellow flags in qualy and things like this," said Sainz.

"It has been a fashion or a tendency of Formula 1 to go to these kind of tracks like Jeddah, Baku recently that are closer to the city - and Miami - but they have more walls and we haven't had any issues with it. The races actually seem to be going quite well to every place we've gone, so it's that similar trend we're going towards."

Predicting the pecking order is anyone's guess but the track layout will suit cars that are strong in the corners - akin to what we saw at the Hungaroring and Zandvoort when McLaren's Lando Norris won.

McLaren and Ferrari will hope to wrestle some momentum back off Mercedes and Kimi Antonelli following the Italian's stunning victory at Monza.

Avoiding a qualifying or race-ending crash for the title contenders this weekend will be pivotal. But we all know F1 drivers will push the limits, but they must all be careful when attacking the new Madring because this track will bite you, and bite hard.

articles.title: Sainz: "Se me hace raro dormir en casa y comer la comida de mi madre"
articles.standfirst: Carlos reconoce lo extraño de estar en el hogar familiar e ir en su coche en una semana de Gran Premio en Madrid
articles.summary: Carlos reconoce lo extraño de estar en el hogar familiar e ir en su coche en una semana de Gran Premio en Madrid
articles.body: Para los madrileños que llevamos más de 20 años cubriendo por el mundo la F1 y nunca haber experimentado la sensación de tener un Gran Premio en la propia ciudad, se hace algo un poco difícil planificar cómo va a ser este fin de semana, yendo a Madring, apenas a 20 minutos o media hora en coche de cualquier punto de la ciudad y dormir en la cama de todos los días. A Carlos Sainz le hace un poco insólita la experiencia también y se lo contaba a MARCA este miércoles, antes de meterse de lleno en la vorágine del circuito. Será una rutina personal inédita para él. "Es algo que estaba pensando esta mañana con mi entrenador. En realidad no hay que cambiar nada, simplemente estoy durmiendo en casa de mis padres efectivamente donde he crecido, eso se hace raro, no te voy a engañar", reconocía en una rueda de prensa de Estrella Galicia 0,0, su patrocinador personal, que ha tenido lugar en la terraza del Cine Callao de Madrid, con vistas al edificio Capitol y su emblemático cartel de Schwepess, tan famoso por 'El Día de la Bestia'. Escenario más madrileño, imposible. "El lunes, cuando llegué a casa y de repente dije bueno, 'es lunes de gran premio pero estoy en casa, es como si me llegara al hotel de Japón o Singapur un lunes y ahora tengo cinco días aquí por delante'. Pero estoy en casa, como la comida de mi madre... esto es muy raro", relataba sonriendo. "Pero bueno, a partir de ahí la rutina no cambia. Voy a hacer exactamente lo mismo, igual me llevo algún coche (propio) al circuito de Madring, por placer, porque no los uso nunca y me gustaría igual darles una vuelta, aunque hoy he venido en mi Golf, el Golf nunca muere, ahí sigue", decía sobre su coche personal con el que se casó el carnet y que tiene 16 años. "Y que más, pues nada, la rutina va a ser la misma, exactamente la misma, simplemente durmiendo en casa con mis padres y teniendo un ambiente igual más familiar, que eso es mejor todavía", expresaba. En realidad, todo está plagado de recuerdos, de antiguos sabores, como en la mesa familiar y de imágenes que le recuerdan a sus primeros pasos en el karting. "Por eso he decidido estrenar este casco, inspirado en el primero que tuve y que era una copia del que usaba mi padre en Citroën en sus años finales en los Rallyes. Muy simple como eran hace 20 años, de la vieja escuela, sin tantas historias como los de ahora. Los que llevaban las leyendas de aquella F1", explicaba sobre su casco para Madring. "Es que cuando tienes 10 o 11 años lo primero que piensas es quiénes son tus ídolos, Fernando, Michael Schumacher, pues ojalá algún día sea como ellos. Pero nunca dices, no, es que si le dices al chaval de 10 o 11 años que corría ahí en Torrejón de Ardoz con ese casco, le llegas a decir no, es que no te preocupes que vas a llegar a Fórmula 1, no te preocupes que vas a correr para McLaren, Ferrari, Williams, Toro Rosso y Renault, no te preocupes que vas a ganar tus primeras carreras con Ferrari, no te preocupes que vas a hacer poles, no te preocupes que vas a llegar y encima vas a conseguir que haya un gran premio en Madrid, que lleva muchos años sin haber". "Pues todo eso son hitos, metas que yo jamás me planteé cuando tenía 10 años, simplemente soñaba algún día con ser piloto de Fórmula 1 y cuando miro ahora para atrás, esos cuántos años han pasado, unos 14, no, mucho más, cuánto ha pasado desde 2005... son 22 años prácticamente, dices que en esos 22 años me hayan pasado todas esas cosas, es algo impensable y por eso me siento tan privilegiado, tan orgulloso de la carrera deportiva alo 32 años...". "Antes que nada, quiero darle la enhorabuena a Kimi por el remontadón y la carrera que hizo, creo que es una carrera para enmarcar y nadie le puede quitar eso. Pero creo que también habéis visto en lo superior que son los coches ahora mismo de cabeza, sobre todo en algunos circuitos, ese Mercedes es todavía bastante superior a todos los demás". "Pero es que la Fórmula 1 es la Fórmula 1 y no sé si os acordaréis hace 3 años cuando Max salía último en Monza y nos ganaba a todos o en Spa y hacía las remontadas, pues este año no lo puede hacer, ¿por qué?... Porque no hay coche". "Es que al final, los pilotos de Fórmula 1 dependemos de nuestra maquinaria, de tener un arma que te permita brillar y lucirte y ahora ese Mercedes permite a Antonelli lucirse y lo está aprovechando para lucirse todo lo que puede y lo está haciendo muy bien".

articles.summary: Brian Vickers broke his silence with a cryptic social media post amid his deep ties to the Jeffrey Epstein files and divorce from Sarah Kellen.
articles.body: Brian Vickers unleashed a rare, cryptic statement via his social media accounts this week, seemingly referring to his ties to Jeffrey Epstein. Not the NASCAR update I was expecting to give today — the second week of 'The Chase' — but this is why you always have to have your head on a swivel in this job. Vickers, 42, appeared all over a batch of released 'Epstein Files' earlier this year — all of them dating back to a time when he was an up-and-coming NASCAR star. A 2003 Busch Series champion, Vickers divorced Sarah Kellen last year. Kellen used to work for Jeffrey Epstein as an assistant, was given immunity years ago, and was subpoenaed by the DOJ last spring. The first time Vickers' name is mentioned in the files is in an email presumably sent by Kellen, and talks about "this NASCAR guy I like" being a "major playboy." There are also several emails to and from Epstein involving Vickers' race team at the time, Michael Waltrip Racing, about a potential issue with Vickers' sponsor, and one particularly disturbing email that was forwarded from Vickers to Epstein with the subject line: "Male Fairy Tale." So that the rest my walk in peace. "I had nothing to do with the mess left by others. If you can not see this you are part of the problem. I wish for peace and yet I am prepared for war against any that threaten my family walking in love. I wish most of all, to say thank you to all who understand and walk the same path. "It is time to build a more gentle world together. But it will not start with tolerance for hate. With unconditional love, not unconditional bounderies." Brian Vickers was a NASCAR Busch Series champion Not sure what prompted that above post, but it's cryptic nonetheless. Vickers and Kellen divorced in 2025 after more than a decade together. Judge Alison Nathan once listed her as "a criminally responsible participant" and the leader of Ghislaine Maxwell. She was one of four women to be granted immunity for the case in 2008. Sarah and Vickers tied the knot back in 2015, right towards the end of Brian's NASCAR career.
